summary:
I hope you’ve been doing good. Have you? How did the novel come out that you told us you were working on? How are all the beautiful chicks who are in love with you? 

I’ve been in bed with double pneumonia for so long now that spiders are building webs around me. What happened was that I had the London flu and then I tried to type up my new novel for Doubleday and it—the flu, not the novel—turned into pneumonia. I went on typing, though, which is a dedication rare in our field; the stupidity, however, I take no credit for—we all have that, working for the pay we work for. Anyhow, I got sicker and sicker, and continued typing, until I finally collapsed. But I finished the novel and sent it off. The thing you do then is go to bed completely, right? No, then I wrote a 6,000 story for Ed Ferman, after which I forget what happened. I remember going from my study into the bedroom and then everything faded out as I hit the floor. I’m bet­ ter now. Ed has the story and Doubleday has the novel. They’ll probably both reject them, which will make a mockery of it all, right? If not an irony and a futil­ ity. However, I feel highly moral. You get a lot after you die when God finds out 
you did all this, right? That is right, isn’t it? Tell me it’s so, Norman; God rewards you for all this, right? Norman, speak up! 

Main reason I’m writing to you, though, is to tell you how much I liked THE IRON DREAM. You maybe saw in the SFWA nomination thing my vote for it for a Nebula, along with Ursul...
